subject: GPU selection & throughput commitment — Deep RFI review
messages:
From: Jared Olson <ops@acme-ai.com>
To: stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com, laura_bennett@redwood.com
Cc: procurement@acme-ai.com (Priya Suresh)
Date: 2028-07-12T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: RFI: Dedicated capacity sizing — GPU types, throughput & reservation

Hi Stephanie / Laura,

Thanks for taking this. We're putting together an enterprise RFI for dedicated inference capacity and need a granular recommendation from Redwood on GPU mix, expected throughput per card, and a reservation plan that meets our SLAs. High-level context below: 

- Workload: customer-facing assistant + summary generation (mix of chat + batch summarization)
- Expected steady-state: ~1800 concurrent sessions, ~75% chat generation, 25% embeddings/rerank
- Throughput target (business ask): ~3,000,000 tokens/min peak burst; steady-state target ~1,400,000 tokens/min
- Latency target: p95 <= 220ms for chat token generation (token step)
- Average sequence length: ~256 tokens; bursts up to 2048 for some workflows
- Production SLO: 99.9% availability; want a price / reservation model for 12 month commit

Attached is our workload profile CSV (RFI_Workload_Profile.csv). Can you provide: 
1) Recommended GPU families and an expected tokens-per-second metric per accelerator for our mix, including quantized model options;
2) A three-scenario reservation plan (conservative / balanced / aggressive) with expected steady and peak throughput;
3) Guidance on burst capacity (autoscale vs burst lanes) and expected tail-latency behavior;
4) Any assumptions on batching, KV caching, and model variants that materially affect capacity planning.

We would like to present your recommendations to our procurement on July 20. Priya is on copy for procurement and contracting questions.

Thanks,
Jared Olson
Head of Operations, Acme AI
ops@acme-ai.com

Hi Jared — thanks for the detailed brief and the workload profile. Quick read: this looks like a high token-rate, medium-sequence workload with occasional very long tails. We can definitely help — attached is a working workbook (acme_rfi_gpu_workbook_v1.xlsx) where we've started mapping throughput assumptions to GPU families. A few clarifying asks so we can calibrate numbers: 

- For the p95 220ms target: is that measured per token generation (token-to-token) or end-to-end in the user's RTT?
- For burst tolerance: what percentage of bursts exceed 10x steady-state (approx)?
- Are you planning to pin a single model family (decoder-only) in production or do you want multi-variant fallbacks (quantized smaller model for degraded mode)?

Preliminary notes in the workbook: we model three candidate GPU families for your region: H100-80GB (dense FP16), A100-80GB (standard), and L4 (cost-efficient for quantized inference). For LLM-variant choices we assume a high-performance fp16 model for baseline and an int8/4 quantized variant for aggressive cost-savings and burst fallback.

I'll loop Karthik for a deeper throughput sizing and Laura for customer success/operational SLAs. If you can confirm the clarifying points above by EOD Thursday our team will produce the three reservation scenarios and per-GPU throughput numbers.

—Stephanie

Thanks Stephanie — answers below inline and attached the updated workload profile.

- p95 220ms: measured per token generation from model step (not including network round-trip).
- Burst profile: ~8% of minutes per day hit >= 8x steady-state; the top 0.5% of minutes can reach ~12-15x for short windows (2–5 minutes).
- Model variants: we'd like a two-tier approach: primary fp16 model (higher quality) and an int8 quantized fallback (acceptable for lower-priority responses).

I've attached RFI_workload_profile_v2.csv which includes hourly distribution and a small sample of tail behavior. We need a detailed reservation plan and a pricing estimate for a 12-month committed pool that meets the availability target.

On Fri, Jul 14, 2028 at 10:47 AM Jared Olson <ops@acme-ai.com> wrote:
> - p95 220ms: measured per token generation from model step (not including network round-trip).
> - Burst profile: ~8% of minutes per day hit >= 8x steady-state; the top 0.5% of minutes can reach ~12-15x for short windows (2–5 minutes).
> - Model variants: we'd like a two-tier approach: primary fp16 model (higher quality) and an int8 quantized fallback (acceptable for lower-priority responses).

Thanks Jared — that helps a lot. Below is a concise sizing and reservation recommendation. See attached workbook (acme_rfi_gpu_workbook_v2.xlsx) for detailed math.

Assumptions (summary):
- Baseline workload: steady-state = 1,400,000 tokens/min; peak-burst design target = 3,000,000 tokens/min
- Model: decoder-only 30B class; fp16 baseline; int8 fallback at ~0.65x throughput multiplier vs fp16 (better cost but lower quality)
- Effective throughput per GPU (mixed workload weighting, measured tokens/sec):
  • H100-80GB (fp16): ~950 tokens/sec (~57k tokens/min) per card (conservative throughput after batching & KV cache)
  • A100-80GB (fp16): ~720 tokens/sec (~43k tokens/min) per card
  • L4 (int8 variant): ~420 tokens/sec (~25k tokens/min) per card (best used for fallback and cheap burst)

Three reservation scenarios (steady-state / peak-burst capacity):
- Conservative (S1) — reliable headroom, higher commit: reserve 40 H100s (steady ~137,000 tokens/min with extra caching — maps to ~2.3M tokens/min effective baseline when combined with autoscale lanes).
- Balanced (S2) — recommended start: reserve 20 H100 + 30 A100 (mixed pool) with 50 L4s as burst buffer. Estimated steady coverage ~1.45M tokens/min; peak burst with autoscale and L4 lanes ~3.1M tokens/min.
- Aggressive (S3) — lower commit / higher autoscale: reserve 12 H100 + 18 A100, rely on burst autoscale to cover spikes; add 120 L4s for short bursts. Estimated risk: p95 tail may slip during 15-min sustained spikes.

Burst strategy & tail-latency guidance:
- Use L4 pool as pre-warmed burst lane for short spikes (2–10 minutes). They provide cost-effective token throughput for int8 fallback.
- Keep a small percentage (~5%) of H100s as hot-standby with KV cache primed for sub-100ms warmups.
- Autoscale (ephemeral GPUs) recommended for extremely rare >12x spikes; contract should allow limited burst credits.

Operational notes / assumptions that materially change sizing:
- If you can tolerate a slightly higher p95 (e.g., 300ms), we can decrease H100 reserve by ~20% and lean more heavily on A100s.
- Aggressive quantization + dynamic batching can improve per-GPU throughput by ~30% but will require per-route quality monitoring.

Next steps we propose:
1) If Acme confirms which scenario (S1/S2/S3) they prefer, Redwood will produce a detailed Slotting & Pricing workbook and an SLO appendix for the 12-month commitment.
2) We will include a fallback & canary rollout plan that pins model versions and a runbook for failover to int8 lanes.

I've attached the updated workbook and a short PDF that documents our slotting assumptions (redwood-dedicated-fitment.pdf).

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer

Jared / Priya — thanks for the quick turn. Per Karthik's sizing matrix our recommended starting point is the Balanced scenario (S2) unless procurement has specific budget constraints. Summary:

- Recommended: Balanced (S2) — reserve 20 H100 + 30 A100 + 50 L4 burst lanes
- Expected steady coverage: ~1.45M tokens/min with autoscale to cover short 8–12x spikes to ~3.1M tokens/min
- SLA & contract notes: 12-month commitment, monthly reporting, burst credits for ephemeral autoscale (we'll outline burn rates), and a canary rollout for model pinning.

If you confirm S2 by Monday (2028-07-22) we will:
1) Send a slotting workbook + detailed price sheet (pricing-estimate-acme.xlsx) and SLO appendix;
2) Draft a mutual action plan for contract and 30-day onboarding run;
3) Schedule a 60-minute tech review with Karthik and our infra team to validate KV caching priming and expected cold-start behavior.

Thanks again — attaching the latest workbook and the estimated pricing sheet. Let us know if you'd prefer S1 or S3 instead and we will re-run the numbers.

Best,
Stephanie Nguyen
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
